Key Characteristics & Etiology: Sudden onset arterial occlusion, most commonly cardiac origin (Atrial Fibrillation, Mitral Stenosis, post-MI mural thrombus).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Circulating embolus lodges at arterial bifurcation (most common femoral bifurcation ~35-40%), causing acute distal ischemia.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: 6 Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Perishingly cold. Red Flag: Muscle rigidity and complete sensory loss (irreversible ischemia).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Handheld Doppler / CT Angiography; ECG/Echo. Management: IV Heparin bolus immediately, emergency Fogarty catheter femoral embolectomy.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute-on-chronic arterial occlusion occurring on pre-existing atherosclerotic plaques.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Plaque rupture or low flow state causes localized thrombosis in narrow diseased vessel.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Gradual onset or sudden worsening of limb pain, history of intermittent claudication, weak/absent contralateral pulses.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Duplex Ultrasound / CT Angiography. Management: IV Heparin, intra-arterial thrombolysis (tPA) or arterial bypass surgery.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Advanced severe peripheral arterial disease in smokers, diabetics, or hypertensive patients.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Progressive multi-segmental arterial stenoses leading to inadequate tissue perfusion at rest.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Ischemic rest pain (worse at night, relieved by dangling leg off bed), non-healing arterial ulcers, gangrene.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: ABPI < 0.5 or ankle pressure < 50 mmHg; CT Angiography. Management: Endovascular angioplasty/stenting or surgical bypass graft.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Ischemic tissue necrosis complicated by superadded bacterial infection (gram-negative / anaerobes).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Bacterial proliferation in dead tissue causes rapid liquefactive necrosis and systemic toxemia.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Blackened, foul-smelling, moist, swollen limb with purulent discharge, crepitus, and severe systemic sepsis/shock.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical inspection; Blood cultures; FBC (marked leucocytosis). Management: Resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, emergency major amputation.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Incompetence of saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal valves due to primary vein wall weakness or pregnancy/standing.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Venous valvular reflux leads to venous hypertension, vessel dilation, tortuosity, and microvascular leakage.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Dilated tortuous veins, leg heaviness, ankle edema, lipodermatosclerosis, active/healed venous ulcers (medial malleolus).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Duplex Ultrasound (gold standard mapping). Management: Compression hosiery, endovenous thermal ablation (EVLA/RFA), foam sclerotherapy, or Trendelenburg operation.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Thrombus formation in deep veins of lower limb driven by Virchow's Triad (stasis, injury, hypercoagulability).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Venous occlusion causes distal venous engorgement, swelling, inflammation, and potential embolization to pulmonary circulation.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Unilateral leg swelling, calf tenderness, warmth, erythema, pitted edema. Red Flag: Dyspnea/chest pain (Pulmonary Embolism).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Wells Score; D-dimer; Duplex Ultrasound. Management: Anticoagulation (LMWH bridged to Warfarin or DOACs for 3-6 months).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Reperfusion injury following prolonged ischemia (>6 hours) during limb revascularization.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Capillary hyperpermeability leads to rapid intracompartmental muscle edema within rigid fascial planes, exceeding capillary perfusion pressure.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe disproportionate pain on passive muscle stretching, tense woody calf compartments, paresthesia.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Intracompartmental pressure measurement (>30 mmHg). Management: Emergency four-compartment leg fasciotomy.
